newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Brokers mull HK downgrade after stocks hit targets.
newsitem.headline: Brokers mull HK downgrade after stocks hit targets.

text.p: Pre-handover euphoria has swept Hong Kong stocks beyond target levels in recent sessions and brokerage firms said on Wednesday they were now considering downgrading Hong Kong in anticipation of a correction.
"I am calling for a 10 to 15 percent correction from the recent highs," said Adrian Faure, research director at Merrill Lynch. "We will reduce our weighting slightly in Hong Kong."
Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule on midnight of June 30 has spurred a frantic scramble for China-related plays, boosting sentiment and liquidity in the territory's market.

"Anecdotal evidence of handover euphoria, red-chip enthusiasm and inflows of capital from China suggest retaining our overweight stance in the regional market allocation may continue to be appropriate for some more time," said Salomon Brothers in a report dated June 10.
"They key question - where does one draw the line between risk and return or prudence and greed?"
The Hang Seng blue chip index jumped beyond Salomon's April 1998 target of 15,000 points earlier this month to reach an all-time high of 15,020.96 on June 3.
Salomon said the index could move well above that level in coming weeks but the odds of a pull-back, or a pause, would rise significantly when the index moved into the 15,700-17,100 range.
"With the index in this region, it would be appropriate to consider reducing the size of our long-held overweight position in Hong Kong," it said.
The Hang Seng Index fell 18.19 points, or 0.13 percent, to 14,421.52 on Wednesday after a drop of 215.42 points on Tuesday.
Faure said this was the beginning of a correction which should bring the index down to fair value of 13,000 points.

Government measures designed to cool down Hong Kong's overheated property market were likely to be imposed after Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule, putting a further dampener on the shares of property development companies, he said.
"I do think in the next three months -- or shorter than that, the next couple of months -- this market is going down certainly to 13,000 and possibly even down as low as 12,000."
While Merrill Lynch would remain overweight in Hong Kong, Faure said it would reduce its current position in favour of Korea and the Philippines.
But while its short term view had turned negative, Faure said Merrill Lynch remained positive on a 12-month stance.

"Assuming interest rates in the U.S. peak in the third quarter this year, with the yield on the U.S. long bond going, we believe, to 6-1/2 percent by the middle of 98, this market could still trade up as far as 16,500 by mid-98."
